Learning language requires learning not only the content of language, but also how to use language to communicate. This paper argues for an extended notion of sublexical modality through an in-depth analysis of three verb classes in Hungarian: verbs of involuntary perception, verbs of involuntary recognition and verbs of physical disposition. Verbs falling into these natural classes pattern together across four, seemingly unrelated, phenomena: the incompatibility with an ability modal auxiliary, the existence of a dispositional middle voice form, the appearance in so-called root infinitives of circumstantial modality, and susceptibility to reinterpretation as auxiliaries. This paper addresses the lack of epenthesis in Baghdadi Arabic within consonant sequences that undergo assimilation vis-à-vis other sequences. The investigation of vowel epenthesis within various types of sequences reveals that heterogeneous final clusters are broken up by epenthesis, whereas final true geminates stay intact. Moreover, false geminates arising from morpheme concatenation do induce epenthesis, but not false geminates arising from total assimilation or heterogeneous clusters arising from partial assimilation. This thesis examines two phonological processes in which vocalic features assimilate to neighboring segments with complex consonant-vowel interactions, namely emphasis spread in Cairene Arabic and lowered larynx assimilation in Buchan Scots. I propose a non-linear analysis in the framework of the Parallel Structures Model (PSM) of feature geometry (Morén 2003). Humans are seemingly unique in the animal kingdom in that we have language; systems enabling communication about any topic, be it past, present or future. In fact, humans are not limited to one language but can acquire several under the right conditions. Although undoubtedly a cultural object, language is also a fundamental part of the mind/brain of a human being, the constitution of which we refer to as a mental grammar. item.title: Approaches to L3 phonological acquisition research: challenges, considerations, best practices
item.dc:creator: Wrembel, Magdalena
item.description:
Wrembel, Magdalena · Zenodo

This contribution aims at a comprehensive overview of state-of-the-art approaches to research on L3 phonological acquisition. The analysis involves theoretical and methodological considerations as well as practical solutions to problems pertaining to the production, perception and processing of speech in third and additional languages. A range of research paradigms, elicitation tasks, and instruments are critically evaluated and various approaches to auditory and acoustic analyses are discussed. The overview is illustrated with examples from current research into L3 phonetics and phonology including the findings from the most recent Polish-Norwegian project.

item.title: Multilingualism and syntactic change in English 1400--1700
item.dc:creator: Ans {van Kemenade}
item.description:
Ans {van Kemenade} · Zenodo

This chapter will bring together recent work on the loss of Verb Second (V2) in English with insights from the literature on the rise of do-support and on the auxiliation of modal auxiliaries. It adds to the discussion of the interrelatedness between these changes, which form a key part of the reorganization of the English verbal system from late Middle English (ME) to the end of early Modern English (EME) and beyond. This complex of changes will also be considered from the perspective of increasing language and dialect contact that I will discuss from the point of view of multilingualism.

This chapter discusses the various uses in a comparative perspective mainly against other Germanic varieties, arriving at an understanding of the wide lexicalization range as reflexes of historical grammaticalization that involves step-by-step cumulative expansion from smaller syntactic structures to bigger ones. item.dc:creator: Svenonius, Peter
item.description:
Svenonius, Peter · Zenodo

In English, auxiliaries linearize in the T position, preceding medial adverbs, while lexical verbs linearize in the verb phrase, following medial adverbs. In a span-based approach to word order, linearization of words in the extended projection is determined by the position of a spell-out label @. The English pattern suggests that the distribution of @ is not a fixed property of a head like T, but is partly dependent on the category of the complement of that head. This first half of the paper presents a novel generalization that the PPI behavior of Russian simplex disjunction is only observed when its alternative with simplex homogeneous conjunction is felicitous and truth-conditionally equivalent to its missing reading. Preschoolers often exhibit difficulties comprehending non-canonical OVS sentences, possibly due to factors related to processing, information structure and/or case marking. In this article, we explore the polysemous Norwegian word senter ‘center’ and similar collective nouns, focusing on their agreement properties. This paper investigates clausal subordination in oral narratives elicited from 72 monolingual Swedish and 102 bilingual Turkish/Swedish children age 4$-$7, keeping task and context constant. The cross-sectional analysis shows a clear increase in the frequency and variety of subordinate clauses with age for both groups, which suggests that children's expressive Swedish language competence in the domain of subordination develops strongly beyond age 4;0, unlike earlier claims in the literature. Young speakers in certain areas of Norway display a word order deviation regarding placement of the subject with respect to verb particles: Both children and teenagers occasionally place verb particles in front of subjects in non-subject-initial clauses, in contrast to the adult pattern. While production data, in particular those including spontaneous speech, have been considered a useful source of evidence in studies of the development of grammar, their adequacy for studies of pragmatic development has been questioned. Production data for pragmatic phenomena are often hard to interpret and typically thought to underestimate children's performance compared to comprehension data. Raquel González Rodríguez
item.description:

Fábregas & González Rodríguez (2020) analyse inhibited events as instances where negation is merged low, over Init(iation)P, with the effect that causation is reinterpreted as inhibition (not-causation) of an event. This predicts that there should be instances of lexical verbs whose initiation layer actually means exerting force to inhibit an event that otherwise was expected to happen. This chapter argues that the prediction is borne out and provides examples from Spanish, showing that their behaviour is the one predicted by the original analysis.

Mian, a Papuan language of Papua New Guinea, shows an unusual system of verb agreement. All finite verbs obligatorily mark subject agreement, yet only a minority of transitive verbs show object agreement. This creates a striking split within the verbal lexicon. item.title: English verb placement in Norwegian/English bilinguals: A Micro-cue approach
item.dc:creator: Anderssen, Merete
Bentzen, Kristine
item.description:
Anderssen, Merete; Bentzen, Kristine · Zenodo

The Micro-cue Model (Westergaard 2009) has been used to explain monolingual first and third language acquisition (Westergaard 2021) but has never been applied to simultaneous bilingual first language acquisition. We fill this gap by considering data on verb placement in English from four bilingual Norwegian/English girls, showing that they display four different patterns of cross-linguistic influence. We argue that the Micro-cue Model is perfect for capturing this variation, as it assumes that the different instantiations of verb placement and residual V2 in English are acquired separately.

This standalone demonstrative is strictly referential, and in general displays common cross-linguistic behaviour. 1 Our focus will be on the other type: the non-agreeing variant, which we dub to, based on its Nominative form.
